c1.story:
Think about the last forty-eight hours of your eating and drinking. A cup of Nescafe, perhaps. A Good Day biscuit with evening tea. A Pepsi on a hot afternoon. A Domino's order on Friday night. A Kingfisher or a peg of Royal Challenge at a friend's place. Maybe a spoonful of sugar from a mill in Uttar Pradesh. Every one of those sits in this industry, and they are four very different businesses wearing the same label.

The first door is the packaged food and dairy brand: Nestle, Britannia, Hatsun, Zydus Wellness. Its genius is turning cheap ingredients, wheat, milk, sugar, into something you buy by name, forever. Few things in Indian business are as durable as a biscuit habit formed in childhood. That is why these companies keep a fat share of every rupee.

The second door is drinks, and it splits in two. Alcohol makers like United Spirits, Radico Khaitan, United Breweries and Allied Blenders sell into a market where every state is a separate country with its own tax, price controls and route to the shop. Soft-drink bottlers like Varun Beverages make PepsiCo's drinks under franchise, and live and die by the summer. Both are bets on people trading up, from regular whisky to premium, from a glass bottle to a can.

The third door is the restaurant chain: Jubilant FoodWorks with Domino's, Devyani with KFC and Pizza Hut. Here the food is cheap and the store is expensive. Rent, staff and delivery-app commissions eat most of the money, so the only number that really matters is whether existing stores sell more this year than last.

The fourth door is the agri processor: sugar mills like Balrampur Chini and EID Parry, LT Foods with Daawat basmati, CCL making instant coffee for other brands. Their year is decided by a crop, a government price and an export notice.

A biscuit habit formed at six can last until sixty. A pizza habit lasts until the next coupon.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each from top to bottom, then compare the profit bars.

  • The name and the line under it explain how each door earns: brands sold at fixed price points through kiranas; alcohol priced and taxed state by state, and soft drinks bottled under franchise; franchised outlets paying rent and royalty; bulk or thin-margin processing.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page.
  • The profit bar is the part to compare. Packaged food and dairy sits at high, because trust and distribution let it price above its ingredients. Drinks sit at medium: premium spirits can earn well, but the state takes most of the shelf price and caps what is left. Restaurants and agri processors both sit at low, for different reasons: restaurants hand their money to landlords, staff and delivery apps; processors hand theirs to the cane price and the crop.
  • The last line is the bet you are making: brand power and soft commodities, premiumisation and state policy, same-store sales and new-store payback, or a crop and a government price.

Then read the so-what line: read the door before you read the multiple. A restaurant chain on a high multiple and a biscuit maker on a similar one are pricing completely different things, store growth and same-store sales in one case, margin stability in the other. Comparing their valuation without knowing the door is comparing a cricket score with a football score.

c2.story:
Every bottle and packet in this industry starts on a farm. Milk comes from millions of small dairy farmers, often a household with two or three animals, collected twice a day through village centres. Wheat comes from mandis and the Food Corporation of India. Sugarcane comes from growers in Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka, paid a price the government sets. Cocoa and coffee beans arrive from abroad or from the plantations of Karnataka and Kerala. Barley, molasses and grain feed the breweries and distilleries.

At the second station, primary processing, the crop becomes a raw material. Cane is crushed into sugar, with molasses and ethanol as by-products. Paddy is milled into rice. Grain or molasses is distilled into neutral spirit, the base of most Indian whisky. Coffee is roasted and turned into instant powder. This station belongs to the sugar mills, the rice millers, CCL and the distilleries of companies like Radico.

The third station is where the magic happens, and the margin. Branded manufacturing turns those raw materials into Maggi, Good Day, Arun ice cream, McDowell's, Kingfisher and Pepsi. It is a short step physically and an enormous one economically.

The fourth station is distribution, and it is where this industry gets strange. A biscuit reaches a kirana through the usual distributor. But a bottle of whisky in Tamil Nadu must be sold to a state corporation that buys all liquor in the state and pays later. In Bihar and Gujarat, prohibition means no legal route at all. Moving a bottle across a state border is a regulatory event, with permits and separate labels, not a logistics one.

In most industries, a state border is a line on a map. In liquor, it is a different market.

The listed brands sit at stations two and three, squeezed between farm prices they cannot control on the left and, for a large chunk of the industry, state-set prices on the right.
c2.read:
Read the top row of boxes left to right, then the band row underneath.

The five boxes are the stations. Farm and commodity sourcing: milk, wheat, cane, paddy, cocoa, coffee, barley and molasses from farmers, cooperatives, importers and the Food Corporation of India. Primary processing: the sugar mills, rice millers, coffee roasters and distilleries. Branded manufacturing: Nestle, Britannia, Hatsun, United Spirits, Radico, United Breweries, Allied Blenders and Varun Beverages. Distribution and retail: state beverage corporations, kiranas, DMart, Blinkit and the outlets of Jubilant and Devyani. And the consumer.

The band row shows the coloured Indian-listed cells under stations two and three. The listed industry is a processing and branding business. The restaurant chains are the exception: they appear at station four, because a Domino's outlet is itself the point of sale.

There is no second band row, because no foreign rival stands across this kitchen. Several of the biggest names, Nestle, United Spirits and United Breweries, are themselves Indian-listed subsidiaries of global parents.

Then read the note: sugar mills cluster in three states, dairies in others, and every state runs its own liquor market. The so-what line is the key to the whole picture. The farm sets the cost on the left and, for liquor and sugar, the state sets the price on the right, so the listed brands earn their keep only where they can price above both. When you look at a company, ask which side of the kitchen squeezes it hardest.

c3.story:
This industry has seven customers, and they are moved by things as different as a heatwave, a state budget and a fuel policy.

The urban household buys noodles, chocolate, coffee, cheese and ready-to-eat meals, and increasingly orders them on a quick-commerce app. It moves with salaries and food inflation. The rural household buys biscuits, milk, tea-time snacks and small bottles of soft drinks, and moves with the monsoon and farm prices. When rural India is squeezed, the five-rupee biscuit pack is where you see it first.

Then the drinkers, a customer unlike any other. They buy whisky, rum, vodka and beer, increasingly premium and craft. They respond to state excise rates, the wedding season and the sheer size of India's young urban population reaching drinking age. Their single biggest driver is a politician in each state capital deciding the tax.

Summer thirst deserves its own tile, because it behaves like a customer. A long, hot April and May sells out soft drinks, beer and ice cream. A rainy April, or an early monsoon, can wipe out a large chunk of the season. In 2025 the monsoon reached Kerala unusually early, and the drinks makers felt it in their June quarter.

The eating-out customer orders pizza, burgers and fried chicken. It is the most discretionary wallet on the list and the first to tighten when urban budgets get squeezed, which is exactly what happened through 2023 and 2024.

Then two customers that are not consumers at all. The oil marketing companies buy ethanol from sugar mills to blend into petrol, at a price the government sets. That single customer has turned many sugar mills into part-energy companies. And export buyers take basmati, instant coffee, sugar and, increasingly, Indian whisky, at the mercy of export rules and trade deals.

The drinker's most important supplier is not the distiller. It is the state finance minister.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who is buying.
  • The second line is what they buy from the industry.
  • The third line is what moves them, which is your watch list outside the industry.

Now sort the tiles by the force that moves them. The weather moves summer thirst and, through the monsoon, rural households. The state moves drinkers, through excise, and oil marketing companies, through the ethanol price. The urban wallet moves urban households and eating out. Trade policy moves export buyers.

Then map each tile to a door from card one. Packaged food leans on urban and rural households. Drinks lean on drinkers and summer thirst. Restaurants lean on eating out, almost entirely. Agri processors lean on oil marketing companies and export buyers, which is why a sugar stock can rally on an ethanol price announcement while consumer stocks fall.

The so-what line gives the practical timing: the summer and the monsoon decide the drinks quarter, the state budget decides the liquor year, and the urban salaried wallet decides the restaurant year. So the IMD's summer forecast in March and the state budgets in February and March are earnings signals for drinks makers, months before results.

c4.story:
Follow a hundred rupees through two businesses that both sell food, and you will see why the market pays such different prices for them.

Start with a packaged food brand. Milk, wheat, sugar, cocoa, coffee and packaging take a little over half of every rupee. Ads, people and distribution take about a quarter. The plant barely registers. What is left is a healthy slice, and it arrives with almost no capital: distributors pay upfront, so the business runs on other people's money. When cocoa or milk spikes, the brand does what every Indian FMCG company does: shrinks the pack before it dares raise the price of the ten-rupee bar.

Now take a restaurant chain. Here the picture flips. The cheese, flour and toppings are cheap, under a quarter of sales. The store is the expensive part: rent, staff, power, delivery commissions and marketing take more than half. Then a heavy block of depreciation and interest, because under the lease accounting rule introduced in 2019, store rents are recorded as a right-of-use asset that depreciates and a lease liability that carries interest. What remains is thin. A restaurant chain is an operating-leverage machine: when same-store sales rise, most of the extra revenue falls to profit because rent and staff are fixed. When they fall, the same leverage works in reverse.

For a food brand, the ingredient is the cost. For a restaurant, the rent is the cost and the food is almost a rounding error.

Liquor has its own twist. Tax is most of the shelf price, and in many states the government also sets the maximum retail price, so a distiller cannot pass on a jump in grain or glass costs until the state approves a new price. Some states take a year. And many state corporations pay late, so working capital at a liquor maker can stretch for months, unlike the food brand that gets paid in advance.

Each door ends up with one number that tells you most of the quarter: gross margin for food, state price approvals for liquor, same-store sales for restaurants.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, one for packaged food and dairy brands and one for restaurant chains. Read each left to right, then compare bar by bar.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is raw materials and packaging. The food brand spends a little over half. The restaurant spends under a quarter. If you stopped here, you would think restaurants were the better business.
  • The opex bar is ads, people, rent and distribution. The food brand spends about a quarter. The restaurant spends more than half. This bar is where the restaurant's money goes.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is a sliver for the food brand and a thick block for the restaurant, roughly five times as tall, because leased stores sit here under lease accounting.
  • The last bar is what remains: a healthy slice for the food brand, a thin one for the restaurant.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below, the list marks which P&L lines matter. Gross margin, excise and state levies, same-store sales and working capital get a clear yes, each tied to a different door. Depreciation, capex, interest and advertising get a sometimes: big for restaurants and bottlers, small for food brands, and for liquor, advertising is restricted by law. The so-what line is the shortcut: one number per door. Know which door you are reading before you pick the number.

c5.story:
Food and beverages has not one cycle but several, stacked on top of each other. Packaged food swings gently with commodity costs and rural demand. Drinks swing with the summer and state taxes. Restaurants swing hard with the urban wallet. And sugar runs on its own cane-and-policy rhythm. The clock on this card shows the combined picture.

The story starts with a jolt. In 2020 lockdowns shut restaurants and liquor shops. When liquor shops reopened in May 2020, queues stretched for kilometres outside them, and households stocked up on noodles and biscuits. It was a strange year rather than a clean bust, which is why the timeline does not paint it as one.

Then the boom. In 2021 and 2022 reopening brought back dine-in and drinking. Jubilant and Devyani boomed on delivery and rapid store expansion, and Varun Beverages scaled across India and Africa. But the boom carried the seeds of the peak: wheat, milk, palm oil and barley costs hit records in 2022, and companies took hard price hikes while restaurant stocks traded at rich multiples.

The bust came in 2023 and 2024. Urban diners pulled back and restaurant same-store sales turned negative. Food inflation slowed packaged food volumes. Sugar mills pivoted harder to ethanol, Nestle and Britannia held margins while volumes lagged, and premium whisky kept growing almost regardless.

2025 was the bottom, and a busy one. Maharashtra raised liquor excise sharply. The India-UK trade deal set out a path to halve the duty on Scotch over time. The September GST cut moved most packaged foods to the lowest slab. And an early monsoon dampened the summer for drinks.

Today the clock reads early up-cycle. Packaged food volumes are recovering on the GST cut and rural demand, premium spirits keep compounding, cocoa and coffee are easing from records, and restaurants are recovering, slowly.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years under each show the last cycle: boom across 2021 and 2022, peak in 2022, bust through 2023 and 2024, bottom in 2025. The arrow points just past the bottom, at early up-cycle, with the detail: GST cut, premium drinks strong, restaurants lagging. That detail is three doors in one line, each at a slightly different point on the clock. Hover an arc for what defined it.

The timeline retells the cycle from 2019, coloured by tone. Notice that 2020 is coloured neutral, not bust: food brands gained as restaurants and bars lost.

The four hands move the arrow, and they disagree in an informative way.

  • Packaged food volume growth: recovering, up arrow. Two quarters of growth would confirm the GST cut and rural demand are real.
  • Restaurant same-store sales: low single digit, flat arrow. Positive but not convincing.
  • Milk, cocoa and coffee costs: easing, up arrow. Good for gross margins.
  • State excise changes: rising in places, a mixed reading. A hike cuts volume in that state; a price approval lifts margin.

Two ups, one flat, one mixed. The so-what line tells you what that means: packaged food and premium spirits benefit first, and restaurant chains need same-store sales to turn clearly positive before they re-rate.

c6.story:
Three dials carry full weight in this industry, and each belongs mainly to a different door.

Food inflation is the packaged food dial. It raises the cost of milk, wheat and sugar, and at the same time squeezes the household budget, a double hit: costs up, volumes down. When food inflation cools, both effects reverse, which is why it is the first number a food analyst checks each month.

Summer heat and the timing of the monsoon form the drinks dial. A long, hot summer sells out soft drinks, beer and ice cream; Varun Beverages builds inventory ahead of it and runs its plants flat out. A cool, wet April does the opposite, and there is no way to sell the lost summer later. Bottlers know this; it is why the IMD's summer forecast in March is read like a results preview.

State excise and pricing policy is the liquor dial. Each state sets its own excise, maximum retail prices and route to market. A hike cuts volumes in that state almost immediately. A delayed price approval traps a distiller's margin when grain or glass costs rise. Maharashtra's sharp excise increase in 2025 showed how quickly a single state budget can reset a large market.

Then the two-dot dials. Cocoa, coffee and barley matter for Nestle, CCL and the brewers: cocoa hit record prices in 2024 and arabica coffee in early 2025, and both are only now easing. Crude oil feeds PET bottles, glass, packaging and freight. Ethanol and sugar policy decide a sugar mill's year: the government's ethanol price, the sugar export quota and the minimum sale price. In December 2023 the government briefly restricted the use of cane juice for ethanol to protect sugar supply, a reminder of how fast this dial can turn. And the monsoon, again, through rural demand for biscuits and milk.

Finally the rupee, which helps exporters of coffee and rice and hurts importers of cocoa and Scotch malt, and interest rates, which slow eating out and de-rate the compounders.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches profits. Notice how many channels name a single door: cocoa and coffee for Nestle and CCL, the shelf price of every bottle for liquor, the ethanol price for sugar mills. This table is really three or four smaller tables interleaved.
  • A rise does: the effect of the dial going up. A green up arrow helps, a red down arrow hurts, and a diamond cuts both ways. Three greens: summer heat, ethanol and sugar policy, and the monsoon. One diamond: the rupee. The rest are red.
  • Weight: one to three dots. Three rows carry three dots: food inflation, summer heat and state excise.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track: food inflation, Brent crude, the rupee and the money-market rate, plus fertiliser output as a proxy for the monsoon's effect on sowing. Two of the three heaviest dials, summer heat and state excise, show a dash. For those you rely on the IMD forecast, state budget announcements and company commentary.

Use the table door by door. For a food brand, read food inflation, cocoa and coffee, and the monsoon. For a drinks maker, summer heat, state excise and crude. For a sugar mill, ethanol and sugar policy and the monsoon. For a restaurant chain, food inflation and interest rates, through the urban wallet. The so-what line gives the shortcut: food inflation for food brands, the summer for drinks makers, state excise for anyone holding liquor.

c7.story:
Why do Indian food and drinks companies not simply grow forever? India eats and drinks more every year, after all. The answer lies in a set of bottlenecks, and the biggest one is a map.

Liquor is the clearest case. India is not one liquor market; it is many. Each state sets its own excise, its own prices, its own licences and its own route to the shop. Some ban alcohol outright: Gujarat has done so for decades and Bihar since 2016. A new government or a state budget can reset a market overnight. A distiller cannot build one national strategy; it must win state by state, and it can lose one at any election.

The second structural bottleneck belongs to restaurants. Rent and delivery-app commissions take a large and rising share of a restaurant's sales. A pizza chain has very little control over what a mall landlord charges or what a food-delivery platform takes per order, and both have tended to go up.

Then the recurring bottlenecks. Milk, wheat and sugar prices follow the monsoon and government support prices, and brands cannot fully hedge them. Sugar mill profits are, in effect, a policy output: the government sets the cane price farmers must be paid, the export quota, the minimum sale price and the ethanol price. The weather is a recurring risk for drinks: a rainy April can cost a chunk of the summer. And slow payments from state beverage corporations in states like Tamil Nadu and Telangana tie up liquor makers' cash for months.

Finally, the two subtler pressures. Liquor cannot be advertised directly, which protects incumbents but makes launching a new brand slow; hence the surrogate ads for soda and music CDs bearing whisky brand names. And health scrutiny of sugar is building slowly. In 2023 an influencer's video attacking the sugar content of Bournvita went viral, and in 2024 the government told e-commerce sites to stop listing such drinks as health drinks.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck, with why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you how to think about each.

  • Structural: permanent. Two rows. State-by-state liquor rules cap the scale any distiller can reach; restaurant rent and delivery cuts cap a chain's margin. Both belong in your valuation.
  • Recurring: four rows. Milk and farm cost swings, sugar and ethanol policy, weather risk for drinks and slow state payments. These are the quarter-level surprises, and between them they touch every door.
  • Two-sided: the advertising ban on liquor. It hurts newcomers and protects incumbents like United Spirits and Radico, so whether it is a risk or a moat depends on which side you own.
  • Slow: health and sugar scrutiny. A slow-building pressure on high-sugar foods and drinks, through labelling rules, possible sugar taxes and public criticism.

Now map rows to doors. Liquor makers face the state rules, the ad ban and slow payments, three rows, which is why their multiples carry a policy discount. Restaurants face rent and delivery cuts. Food brands face farm costs and health scrutiny. Sugar mills face policy and the monsoon. Bottlers face the weather.

The so-what line tells you which are worth a news alert: the weather and policy notices, because they arrive without warning. State liquor rules and farm costs set the ceiling; they do not surprise, they constrain.

c8.story:
Few industries answer to as many rule-makers as food and drink. And in this one, the rules do not just shape the business; in places, they are the business.

Start with the food safety regulator. In June 2015 FSSAI ordered Maggi noodles off the shelves after tests alleged excess lead. Nestle India pulled the product, wrote off stock and watched a brand that had owned the instant-noodle category for decades disappear for five months. Maggi came back by the end of 2015 and regained its lead, but the episode taught every food company what a single regulatory order can do. Today FSSAI is working on front-of-pack nutrition warnings for sugar, salt and fat, which would put a very different message on the front of a biscuit or chocolate pack.

Then the state excise departments, the most powerful regulators in the liquor business. They set the tax, the maximum retail price, licences and how a bottle reaches the shop. For a distiller, the state excise policy is effectively the business plan.

The GST Council moved most packaged foods to the lowest slab in September 2025, a price cut that cost the companies nothing. Aerated drinks remain in the highest slab, and any move towards a broader sugar tax would hit soft drinks hard.

For sugar mills, two rulebooks dominate. The Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution sets the sugar export quota, the minimum sale price and stock limits. The ethanol blending programme has the oil companies buying ethanol at a government-set price to mix into petrol, which has turned many mills into part-energy companies with a steadier income.

And trade deals now matter. The India-UK agreement signed in 2025 cuts the duty on Scotch in phases. Cheaper imported Scotch competes with Indian premium whisky, but it also cuts the cost of the Scotch malt that Indian blenders import. Like many rules in this industry, it cuts both ways.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you care, and its status.

  • New: the GST Council's slab cut and the India-UK trade deal. The first is lifting packaged food volumes now; the second will play out over years as Scotch duty falls in phases.
  • Live: the consumer affairs ministry's sugar controls, the ethanol blending programme and the food-processing incentive scheme. The first two decide a sugar mill's year; the third is a modest tailwind for processing capex.
  • Always: state excise departments and APEDA with DGFT. State excise is the single biggest driver of liquor volumes and margins. APEDA and DGFT set export registrations, minimum export prices and bans on rice and sugar.
  • Coming: FSSAI's front-of-pack labelling and its move to hold online food players accountable. A slow risk for high-sugar, high-salt products.

Map the rows to doors. Packaged food answers to FSSAI and GST. Liquor answers to state excise and the trade deal. Sugar mills answer to the consumer affairs ministry, the ethanol programme and export rules, three rows, which is why sugar stocks trade on policy headlines more than on demand. Restaurants barely appear here; their rules are landlords and delivery apps.

The row to watch closest is state excise, marked always for a reason: it never goes away, and every February and March, as states present budgets, it can move. Dated regulatory news for this industry sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces ask one question: once the money comes in, who keeps it? The answer in food and beverages depends almost entirely on whether you sell a packet or a plate.

Start with the packaged food brand. Rivalry exists, but most food categories have one or two dominant brands, and they compete through ads and launches rather than price wars. Suppliers are millions of milk and wheat farmers with little pricing power individually. Buyers barely negotiate: a shopper picking up Maggi does not haggle over two rupees. Newcomers face a wall of trust and distribution that took decades to build. Substitutes exist, local snacks and home cooking, but the habit is powerful.

Now the restaurant chains and processors, grouped on the other side of the radar. Rivalry is intense: a pizza chain fights dozens of other chains, cloud kitchens and local restaurants, all one tap away on the same delivery app. Sugar mills sell a commodity. Suppliers bite hard: restaurant landlords raise rents, delivery apps take commissions, and the government sets the cane price a mill must pay. Buyers switch easily: a diner moves for a coupon, a sugar buyer for a paisa. Newcomers can enter quickly: a new pizza brand or cloud kitchen can open in months. And the biggest substitute is the oldest: cooking at home.

A restaurant's fiercest rival is not the chain across the road. It is the kitchen at home.

Drinks sit between the two, though they are not drawn separately. Premium spirits enjoy brand loyalty and an advertising ban that protects incumbents, but the state takes most of the price and caps what is left. Bottlers have the PepsiCo brand but depend on the franchisor's terms.

The result is the ranking the so-what line describes: packaged food keeps the most, drinks keep a good share where states let them price, and restaurants and processors keep the least.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force exerts. So a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: packaged food and dairy brands, and restaurants with processors. Look at size first. The packaged food shape sits inside the other on every spoke. It hugs the centre on buyers, its lowest score, and stays modest on suppliers, entrants and substitutes. The restaurants-and-processors shape reaches the outer ring on rivalry and pushes well out on suppliers and entrants.

The shapes do not cross. There is no force on which restaurants and processors have the easier life. The gap is about the same on four spokes, rivalry, suppliers, buyers and entrants, which tells you the weakness is everywhere rather than in one place: landlords and delivery apps on one side, coupon-hunting diners on the other, and low barriers to new competitors all round. The narrowest gap is on substitutes, because home cooking and local snacks substitute for both doors.

The table beside the radar gives each score from zero, no pressure, to three, heavy pressure, with a reason. Note that the second shape combines two very different businesses, restaurants and sugar mills, which happen to score similarly for different reasons. When you apply it to a single company, adjust. A sugar mill's supplier spoke is really the government cane price. A restaurant's supplier spoke is really its landlord and the delivery platform. A drinks maker, not drawn here, would sit between the two shapes, with the state as a powerful extra force the radar does not show. Redraw the shape for the company you hold; that is the point of the framework.

c10.story:
A food and beverage results call can cover biscuits, beer and burgers in the same breath. Eight numbers cut through it, but which ones matter most depends on the door.

Underlying volume growth comes first: how much more was sold, stripped of price hikes. For food, mid-single-digit volume growth or better is healthy; for premium spirits the bar is higher. Management usually says it on the call. Price-led growth with flat volumes is a brand being milked.

Gross margin is the commodity squeeze versus pricing power. For a food brand, it is the first place a spike in milk, cocoa or wheat shows up. EBITDA margin then shows what is left after ads, rent and distribution, with a catch for restaurants: under the lease accounting rule, rent disappears from EBITDA into depreciation and interest, which flatters the margin. Analysts often look at restaurant margins before the rule to compare like with like.

Then the door-specific numbers. Same-store sales growth is the one number for restaurant chains: are existing outlets selling more than last year? Premium share of volume is the one number for spirits and beer: is the mix shifting towards the higher-priced brands that carry fatter margins? United Spirits and Radico have built their investment cases on that shift.

Receivable days tell you something peculiar to liquor: how late the state corporations are paying. A rise is not a sign of weak demand; it is a sign that a state government is short of cash. Inventory days matter for food brands, where low is good, and for sugar mills, which by nature sit on a large stock after the crushing season and should see it fall as the year goes on.

Finally, return on capital. The best food brands earn extraordinary returns, because they need almost no capital to grow. A restaurant chain's test is whether new stores earn enough to justify opening more.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask. Some rows apply to every company; same-store sales, premium share and receivable days each belong mainly to one door.
  • What good looks like is the benchmark, often split by door: food, spirits and restaurants get separate marks for EBITDA margin; food and bottlers for gross margin; food and sugar mills for inventory days. Always use the mark for the right door. Note the restaurant EBITDA mark is quoted before the lease accounting rule, so check which basis a company reports on.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of the industry's listed companies in our database. It appears for gross margin, EBITDA margin, receivable days, inventory days and return on capital. Volume growth, same-store sales and premium share show a dash, because companies give them in commentary and presentations rather than in a standard line.

A caution: the median blends food brands, liquor makers, restaurant chains and sugar mills, businesses with completely different shapes. It is a weather report for the label, not a benchmark. The better comparison is three-way: the company's own number, its door's good mark, and its own trend. One habit worth building for liquor names: always read receivable days alongside volume, because a liquor maker with strong volumes and stretching receivables is selling well to a state that is not paying.

c11.story:
The best warnings about a food and beverage quarter come from the weather office, the commodity screens, the state budgets and the delivery apps, long before the companies report.

The earliest voices speak two quarters ahead. Cocoa and arabica coffee futures matter because beans are contracted ahead: the price paid today arrives in a chocolate maker's or coffee roaster's costs about two quarters later. The monsoon and cane acreage matter for sugar: cane planted today is the sugar and ethanol a mill will produce in the coming season.

One quarter ahead, a trio. The IMD's summer heat forecast tells bottlers and brewers whether to stock up, and a hot forecast usually means a strong June quarter. Milk procurement prices reset dairy and chocolate costs about a quarter later. And ethanol tender price announcements set the distillery margins of sugar mills for the season.

Then the same-quarter signals. State budgets and excise notifications move liquor volumes within the month. And food-delivery order growth at Eternal and Swiggy tracks restaurant chain sales almost in real time; if the platforms report slowing food delivery, Jubilant and Devyani's numbers are unlikely to surprise on the upside.

Put them together and you get the rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when food volumes are growing, soft commodity costs are stable or falling, and restaurant same-store sales are positive. Today two of the three tick: food volumes are growing on the GST cut and rural demand, and cocoa and coffee are off their highs. The third does not convince: restaurant same-store sales are barely positive. Two of three means early recovery. That is why the call favours brands with pricing power and a premium mix, and suggests waiting for clear same-store sales growth before turning to restaurant chains.

The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read the channel.

  • The middle, one quarter ahead: the IMD summer heat forecast, milk procurement prices and ethanol tender prices. One for drinks, one for dairy, one for sugar.
  • Far left, the same quarter: state budgets and excise notifications, and delivery-app order growth. These confirm rather than warn, but they are fast: excise moves liquor within the month, and delivery data tracks restaurants in near real time.

Notice that almost every dot belongs to a single door. Use the chart that way: if you hold a chocolate or coffee name, start on the far right; if you hold a bottler, the middle; a liquor maker, the far left; a restaurant chain, the delivery dot.

Below the chart sits the three-sign rule. Two ticks: food volumes growing, with the GST cut and rural demand behind them, and soft commodity costs easing, with cocoa and coffee off their highs. One cross: restaurant same-store sales, barely positive and not convincing. Two of three reads as early recovery.

The call box gives the view, its three points, and what would change it: a milk or cocoa spike, a wave of state excise hikes or a new prohibition, and a weak monsoon that stalls rural demand and cuts cane. Treat those as alerts; if one appears, the call is due a rethink.
